15: // ResourceInstanceObject is the local representation of a specific remote
16: // object associated with a resource instance. In practice not all remote
17: // objects are actually remote in the sense of being accessed over the network,
18: // but this is the most common case.

20: // It is not valid to mutate a ResourceInstanceObject once it has been created.
21: // Instead, create a new object and replace the existing one.
22: type ResourceInstanceObject struct {
23: 	// Value is the object-typed value representing the remote object within
24: 	// Terraform.
25: 	Value cty.Value
26: 
27: 	// Private is an opaque value set by the provider when this object was
28: 	// last created or updated. Terraform Core does not use this value in
29: 	// any way and it is not exposed anywhere in the user interface, so
30: 	// a provider can use it for retaining any necessary private state.
31: 	Private []byte
32: 
33: 	// Status represents the "readiness" of the object as of the last time
34: 	// it was updated.
35: 	Status ObjectStatus
36: 
37: 	// Dependencies is a set of absolute address to other resources this
38: 	// instance dependeded on when it was applied. This is used to construct

40: 	// longer available, such as if it has been removed from configuration
41: 	// altogether, or is now deposed.

45: 	// create_before_destroy option when this instance was last updated.
46: 	// Because create_before_destroy also effects the overall ordering of the

63: 	// update, or delete operation. Since it cannot be moved into the
64: 	// ObjectRead state, a tainted object must be replaced.

86: // will be stored correctly. The caller must also provide the version number
87: // of the schema that the given type was derived from, which will be recorded
88: // in the source object so it can be used to detect when schema migration is
89: // required on read.

92: // so the caller must not mutate the receiver any further once once this

96: 	// structure with UnknownAsNull, and save the PathValueMarks
97: 	// so we can save them in state.

part.text:
All done. Summary of the fix:

**Root cause:** cty's `SetVal` transfers marks from set elements up to the containing set (set elements cannot be individually marked, since that would change set identity). So when the planned value was marked with element-level paths (e.g. `[get_attr set_block, IndexStep{...}]`), the actual value carried a *collection-level* mark, and state stored `[get_attr set_block]`. On the next plan, core compared the raw schema-derived element-level path list against the state-derived collection-level path, saw a mismatch, and forced a spurious `Update`. Additionally, computed nested attributes unknown at plan time were never marked, so apply recorded no sensitive paths at all.

**Changes** (all in `internal/terraform/`):
- `marks.go` — removed the now-unused `filterMarks` helper.
- `node_resource_abstract_instance.go`:
  - `plan` (node_resource_abstract_instance.go:1223): the NoOp check now compares marks *derived from the actual values* (`UnmarkDeepWithPaths` on the planned value vs `priorPaths`), which normalizes the set mark-transfer, instead of comparing a pre-computed path list via `filterMarks`.
  - `apply` (node_resource_abstract_instance.go:2498): always adds all marks to the applied value — the plan's `afterPaths` plus schema-derived sensitive paths computed from the (unmarked) provider-returned new value — so computed attributes that were unknown during planning still get recorded in state.
  - `refresh` (node_resource_abstract_instance.go:726): same unmark → union → re-mark pattern, so schema marks can be safely derived even if the provider returned marked values.

**Validation:** the two in-tree evaluation tests (`TestContext2Plan_nestedSensitiveMarks`, `TestContext2Apply_sensitiveNestedComputedAttributes`) now pass, an end-to-end apply/apply/plan reproduction of the reported issue shows NoOp with state matching the reported format, and the full `internal/terraform`, `states`, `plans`, and `configs` suites pass with no regressions.
